title: Taking and learning from a practice exam
author: ab-strategy-author
summary: How to sit a Liminal practice exam under the conditions of the AP® Calculus AB Exam, mark your confidence as you answer, write down the raw points you expect before you see the key, and then turn every lost point into a dated next task: a cold redo before reading solutions, an honest rubric check, an error log by unit and cause, a route from each cause to a specific page of this course's exam preparation, and a comparison with your earlier forms in raw points only.

blocks.text: A full practice exam takes more than three hours, and most of its value comes afterward, from what you change because of it. Sitting form after form without that step mostly rehearses what you can already do. One cycle runs about a week:

blocks.caption: One practice-exam cycle.
head: When
What you do
rows: Sit the form under exam conditions. Mark each multiple-choice answer S, U or G as you go. When time ends, write down the raw points you expect, part by part.
Mark multiple choice from the key's letters only. Redo every miss and every U or G item cold, then read the key's reasons, then check free response against the rubrics and fill in the error log.
Work the next task each log row names, and redo every missed item cold once more on its retry date.
Compare raw points by part, section and unit, and compare each expectation with what you earned.

blocks.text: Liminal has four practice exams for this course, A to D. The review plans on the exam-preparation page space them several weeks apart, with none in the last four days before the exam, so that each form has time to change what you study next.

Take the whole form in one sitting when you can: 3 hours 10 minutes of working time. Concentration and pacing in the last hour are part of what you are practising. When one long block is impossible, take Section I (1 hour 40 minutes) and Section II (1 hour 30 minutes) as two sittings a day or two apart, as the course's week 33 does, and never split a part. Two sittings still give honest raw points by part, but they cannot show how you work when tired, so take at least one form, ideally your last, in one sitting.

blocks.text: On the exam itself, delivery is hybrid digital: you answer multiple choice and read the free-response prompts in the Bluebook app, and you handwrite free-response answers in a paper booklet. Bluebook's built-in Desmos graphing calculator appears only in the two calculator parts, and up to two approved handheld calculators may also be used. At least two free-response questions use real-world contexts. (College Board's exam and calculator-policy pages, checked 2026-10-22.) Liminal's practice exams are printed.

items: Print the student copy. Answer multiple choice on its answer sheet, keeping the margin for the marks described below, and handwrite free response in the space under each part, as you will in the paper booklet.
Use a timer you cannot pause, and stop when a part's time ends. If you want to finish an item afterward, switch to a different color; that work does not count toward the raw points.

Use the calculator only in Section I Part B and Section II Part A, set to radians, and keep it out of reach during the other two parts. Practise with the calculator you will use on the exam: Desmos if you plan to rely on Bluebook's, your handheld if you plan to bring one.

No notes, formula sheet, textbook or phone. Liminal's practice exams are taken without a formula sheet; College Board's exam pages, checked 2026-10-22, do not mention one. A form taken with notes open measures the notes.

Know Liminal's practice scoring before you begin. Each multiple-choice question is worth 1 raw point and nothing is taken off for a wrong choice, so answer every question. Liminal scores each free-response question out of 9 points, so Section I holds 42 raw points and Section II holds 54.

blocks.text: Pausing the clock to look something up, or finishing a part with extra time, and then comparing those raw points with a form taken under the rules.
blocks.fix: Keep one set of conditions for every form: timed, closed-book, calculator only where allowed. Then a change between forms reflects a change in you, not in the conditions.

blocks.text: In the margin of the answer sheet, beside each multiple-choice answer, write one letter.

head: Mark
Meaning
rows: You would bet on it: you worked it and checked it, or you know the fact.
You worked it but doubt a step, or you narrowed it to two choices.
You chose without a method that reached an answer.

blocks.text: Mark as you answer, not at the end. A mark written after you have seen later questions, or the key, records hindsight rather than confidence. Each mark costs a second and does two jobs later: it picks out the right answers that still need a redo, and it shows whether your sense of sure matches your results. In free response, write a small U beside any part where you doubt the method or the justification.

Write the clock time beside the last question of each part, and circle the number of any item you skip to come back to. Section I Part A allows about 2.1 minutes a question and Part B about 2.9; Section II averages 15 minutes a question. These notes are what let you tell a time error from a knowledge error afterward. The pace is an average and fails as a rule for any single item: a quick item banks time for a long one. The guide How the exam runs and how to pace it has the pacing plan.

When the last part ends, and before you open the key, write your predicted raw total for each part: Section I Part A out of 29, Part B out of 13, Section II Part A out of 18 and Part B out of 36. Students tend to stay overconfident from exam to exam, partly because they do not use their own earlier results (Foster et al. 2017). A written expectation, later set beside the result, is what lets you correct for that.

sections.title: After: within one or two days

blocks.text: Do the analysis within a day or two, while you still remember why you chose what you chose. Keep every solution closed until step 3.

items: Mark multiple choice from the key's letters alone, without reading rationales. Circle every wrong answer.

Redo cold. On a fresh page, untimed and closed-book, rework every missed item and every item marked U or G, including those you got right. Start with the sure-but-wrong items. Add every free-response part you left unfinished or marked U. Use the calculator only where the original part allowed it.

Then open the key. For each redone item, read the rationale and the steps, and for a wrong choice read the note on the letter you picked, which names the error that produces it. Read for why each step is valid, not only for the answer.
Check free response against the rubric, row by row, as described below.
Fill in the error log, and give every row a next action and a retry date.

blocks.text: Why this order. Making an error and then getting corrective feedback helps learning, and errors made with high confidence are among the easiest to correct once the right answer is shown (Metcalfe 2017). So the sure-but-wrong items come first; they are also the ones you would otherwise never look at again. Feedback that explains why an answer is right helps more on new questions than feedback that only gives the answer (Butler, Godbole & Marsh 2013), so read the steps, not just the letter. The cold redo comes before the key because it sorts your errors: what you fix alone, untimed, points to time, reading, the calculator or a slip; what you cannot fix points to a concept or a method.
Spending half an hour on a cold redo of an item you cannot start.
blocks.fix: Cap a cold redo at about 5 minutes for a multiple-choice item and 10 minutes for a free-response part. If no method has started by then, write down how far you got and open the key. Being unable to start is itself the diagnosis: a concept or a method choice.

blocks.prompt: After a form you wrote down an expected 34 raw points for Section I. Scoring from the key's letters, you missed items 4, 11, 17, 23, 31 and 38. Your margin marks on those were S on 4 and 31, U on 11, 17 and 38, and G on 23. Among the items you got right, you had marked 8 and 35 U and 26 G; every other right answer was marked S. In Section II you marked part 2(c) U and left part 5(d) unfinished. (a) How many Section I raw points did you earn, and what does the gap from your expectation tell you? (b) List what goes into your cold redo, in the order you would start it.
blocks.hint: Every item marked U or G is redone, right or wrong, and so is every free-response part marked U or left unfinished.
blocks.answer: (a) 36 of 42 raw points, 2 more than the 34 you expected: the expectation was too low, which is also a calibration error worth tracking. (b) Eleven entries. Start with items 4 and 31, the sure-but-wrong ones. Then the other misses, 11, 17, 23 and 38; the right answers marked U or G, 8, 26 and 35; and the free-response parts 2(c) and 5(d).
steps: Section I has 42 items, one raw point each, and you missed 6: 42 − 6 = 36 raw points.
36 − 34 = 2, so you expected 2 points fewer than you earned. Underconfidence also means your sense of your own work is off.
Items 4 and 31 were marked S and missed: confidence and result disagree most there, so they come first.
The other misses are 11, 17 and 38 (marked U) and 23 (marked G).
Right but not secure: 8 and 35 (U) and 26 (G). A shaky or lucky answer will not reliably repeat, so they are redone too.
Free response: 2(c), marked U, and 5(d), unfinished. In all, 2 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 11 entries.
For later: 33 of your 35 S marks were right, so 2 sure answers in 35 were wrong.

blocks.text: Check free response honestly. The rubric awards points for what is on the page, so read your page the way a stranger would.

items: Check each rubric row on its own. A point you would have earned if you had written something more is a point lost.

A setup point needs the setup in mathematical notation: the integral with its limits, integrand and differential, or the equation being solved. A calculator result alone earns at most what the rubric gives for the answer.
A justification point needs the reason, named: the function and its sign or sign change, or the theorem with its hypotheses checked.

Check every equals sign. An approximation written with =, or two different quantities chained with =, is a false statement, and Liminal's rubrics can withhold a point for it even when the number is right.
Credit one answer per part. If two answers to a part are left standing, credit neither. A false extra statement in a justification loses that justification point, even beside a correct reason.
Where the rubric credits later work that is consistent with an earlier wrong answer, apply it; where it does not, do not invent the credit.

When you cannot tell whether a row is earned, do not award it, and log why. If you can, trade one question with a classmate and check each other's; a second reader shows how generous you are with yourself.

blocks.prompt: A calculator free-response part reads: "Wax flows into a vat at W(t) = 24 + 10 sin(√(3t)) liters per hour for 0 ≤ t ≤ 6. At t = 0 the vat holds 150 liters. How many liters of wax are in the vat at t = 6?" Its rubric: 1 point for a definite integral of W(t) from 0 to 6; 1 point for adding the initial 150 liters; 1 point for the answer, correct to three decimal places, with units. A student wrote: "150 + ∫ from 0 to 6 of W(t) dt = 296.960 liters." Award the points row by row, name the cause of each lost point, and say what a cold redo would show.
blocks.hint: Evaluate the integral yourself in radian mode, then in degree mode.
blocks.answer: 2 of 3 points. The setup and the initial amount are earned. The answer point is lost: the vat holds 150 + 150.859 ≈ 300.859 liters. 296.960 is what the calculator gives in degree mode, so the cause is the calculator. A cold redo in radian mode gives 300.859, which confirms that the method was sound.
steps: Setup: "∫ from 0 to 6 of W(t) dt" has the integrand, both limits and dt, so that row is earned.
Initial amount: 150 + … is written, so that row is earned.
Answer: in radians, ∫ from 0 to 6 of W(t) dt ≈ 150.859, so the amount is ≈ 300.859 liters. With the sine read in degrees, the integral is ≈ 146.960 and the total ≈ 296.960, the student's value.
Total: 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 of 3.
Log row: calculator, degree mode. Next action: the calculator skills guide, and a check of radian mode written as the first step of every calculator part.

blocks.text: Give every lost point a row: one row per multiple-choice item or free-response part, and a second row when a part lost points for a second, separate reason. Log a right answer you marked U or G too, with 0 points lost; it is knowledge you cannot count on yet. The unit is the item's first topic in the key, which is also how the key's tally counts it.

blocks.caption: Seven causes. Choose the one whose fix would have saved the point.
head: Cause
What it looks like
What the cold redo shows
rows: You did not know or misremembered an idea: what a theorem needs, what a test concludes, what a derivative or an integral means in context.
You still cannot do it alone, and the key's reason is new to you.

You know the methods but picked the wrong one: disks where washers were needed, the Mean Value Theorem where the Intermediate Value Theorem was needed, the second derivative test where it says nothing.
Once you know which method to use, you finish quickly.
Right method, slip in carrying it out: a sign, a chain-rule factor, the limits after a substitution, arithmetic.
You get it right on the redo, or you find the slip by checking your own steps.
You answered a different question: f for f′, relative for absolute, an interval for a single time, a net change for an amount, or a misread graph or table.
You get it right as soon as you reread the last line of the prompt.
The mathematics was right but the page did not earn the point: a missing setup, an unnamed reason, a false equality, missing units, calculator syntax.
Your answer matches the key, but a rubric row is not met by what you wrote.
Degree mode, a value rounded too early, a mistyped function, or no calculator where one was needed.
A careful calculator redo gives the key's value.
You did not reach the item, or rushed it; your clock notes show that the part ran out.
You solve it untimed at a reasonable pace.

blocks.text: When two causes fit one point, log the earlier link in the chain: a concept gap that led to a slow, confused attempt is a concept error, not a time error. The categories fail when you honestly cannot tell which applies. Then pick the one with the more useful next action, and let the retry confirm or correct it.

A log changes nothing by itself. In one classroom study, students who filled in reflection forms after exams, with nothing following from them, did no better on later exams and judged their own learning no better (Soicher & Gurung 2017). What helps is the task the reflection leads to, so every row gets a specific task on this course's exam-preparation page and a date.

blocks.text: Put every missed item back on the calendar 2 to 7 days later, and redo it cold again. A retry the next day mostly tests short-term memory; one left for weeks may not happen before the next form. On the retry, also do one fresh item of the same kind from a unit review or a mixed set, because a repeated item can turn into remembering its answer rather than solving it.

Work first on the cause that cost the most points, but not only on that one. This rule fails when the biggest cause is time: running out of time often comes from slow procedures earlier in the part, so read your clock notes before you treat it as a pacing problem.

blocks.prompt: On Section I Part A you marked an item asking for ∫ (4x − 5)/(x^2 + 9) dx as S, and your choice was wrong: you had set u = x^2 + 9 for the whole fraction. In the cold redo you tried the same substitution and stalled on the −5. When the key's first step split the integrand into 4x/(x^2 + 9) − 5/(x^2 + 9), you finished in two minutes. Name the cause, a next task on the exam-preparation page, and a retry window.
blocks.hint: Ask what the key's first line gave you that you did not already have.
blocks.answer: Method choice. Next task: a timed mixed set, writing the technique's name before solving each item, plus the unit 6 review's section on choosing a technique. Retry this item cold between day 2 and day 7.
steps: Once the split was given, you carried out both pieces correctly and quickly, so the substitution and the arctangent pattern are sound.
You know both techniques but did not see that the fraction needed splitting, which is a method-choice error rather than a concept or procedure error.
Choosing a technique is trained by mixed practice, where deciding what applies is part of every item; writing the technique's name first makes the choice visible.
For reference: ∫ (4x − 5)/(x^2 + 9) dx = 2 ln(x^2 + 9) − (5/3)arctan(x/3) + C.
It was sure but wrong, so it belonged at the front of the redo list.

blocks.prompt: A free-response part gave the graph of g′ on [0, 7] and g(0) = 4, and asked for the absolute maximum value of g on [0, 7]. You wrote: "g′ changes from positive to negative at x = 3, and g(3) = 9 is greater than g(0) = 4 and g(7) = 6, so the absolute maximum is at x = 3." You lost the answer point. In the cold redo, after rereading the prompt, you wrote at once "the absolute maximum value is 9". Classify the error, give a next task, and say what result of the redo would have changed the classification.
blocks.hint: Compare what the prompt asked for with what your last sentence gave.
blocks.answer: Reading the question: the part asked for a value, and you gave the input where it occurs. Next task: on the next mixed set and workshop set, underline what each prompt asks for and check your last sentence against it. If the redo had again chosen x = 3 by the sign change alone, without comparing the endpoints, the cause would be concept, and the next task would be the candidates test in the unit 5 review.
steps: Your work compared the right candidates, so the method and the justification were sound.
"At x = 3" names an input; "the maximum value" asks for an output of g. The answer the part wanted was 9.
You corrected it unaided as soon as you reread the prompt, which is the mark of a reading error.
Rewritten answer: g is continuous on [0, 7], and the candidates are g(0) = 4, g(3) = 9 and g(7) = 6, so the absolute maximum value of g on [0, 7] is 9.

blocks.text: From the second form on, set the new raw points beside the old ones by part, by section and by unit, and set each expectation beside its result. Liminal's practice exams give every unit the same number of multiple-choice questions on every form (5 each for units 1, 2, 4 and 8; 3 each for units 3 and 7; 8 each for units 5 and 6), so those unit counts compare directly. Free-response points by unit vary from form to form.

blocks.text: Calibration. Subtract each result from its expectation. A gap that shrinks across forms suggests your judgment of your own work is improving, which matters on the exam itself when you decide which answers to check. Do the same with your S marks: if more than about 1 in 10 sure answers are wrong, check an answer before you mark it S. With only a handful of S marks that fraction jumps with a single item, so read it over two forms.

Read the comparison for patterns, not single numbers. Forms differ in difficulty, and a unit with three multiple-choice questions can move two points on one lucky guess and one slip. Trust a change that shows up on two forms and agrees with the causes in your log. Do not retake the same form to compare, since you will partly remember it.
The shares of exam score in the format table describe the real exam. They are not a formula to apply to Liminal's raw points, which stay raw, by part, as practice evidence.

blocks.prompt: Use the example comparison above. (a) Your sure answers were right 19 of 24 times on form A and 22 of 25 times on form B. By the 1-in-10 guideline, should you still check an answer before you mark it S? (b) Unit 3 multiple choice went from 1 of 3 to 3 of 3, and unit 6 from 4 of 8 to 6 of 8. Which change is stronger evidence of improvement, and how much should either move your plan on its own?
blocks.hint: For (a), count the wrong S answers on each form and over both forms. For (b), count the questions each change rests on, not the percentages.
blocks.answer: (a) Yes. 5 of 24 sure answers were wrong on form A (about 21%) and 3 of 25 on form B (12%): fewer, but still more than 1 in 10, and 8 of 49 (about 16%) over both forms. Keep checking before you mark S. (b) Neither is clearly stronger: each rests on just two more questions right. On its own, neither should move a unit in the plan; let the retries of each unit's logged items decide.
steps: Wrong S answers: 24 − 19 = 5 on form A and 25 − 22 = 3 on form B.
5/24 ≈ 0.21 and 3/25 = 0.12. Both are above 0.10, the guideline's 1 in 10.
With so few S marks, one item moves the fraction by about 4 percentage points, so read the two forms together: 8 wrong out of 49, about 16%. The trend is good, but the habit of checking should stay.
Unit 3 rose from 33% to 100% and unit 6 from 50% to 75%, but both changes are two questions, which one guess and one slip could produce. Percentages on a few questions exaggerate change.

blocks.text: Write each log entry, and any comment on a classmate's work, about the mathematics, not about the person. Feedback that turns attention toward the self rather than the task often fails to help and sometimes hurts (Kluger & DeNisi 1996). A cause that names a step can be fixed; a verdict about a person cannot.

blocks.prompt: The cause column for a missed volume question
blocks.text: Method choice: I used discs, but the region does not touch the axis of rotation, so each slice is a washer with inner radius equal to the distance from the axis to the nearer curve.
Log entries such as "bad at related rates" or "careless again".
blocks.fix: Name the step that failed and the correct step. "Careless" is not a cause: if it keeps happening, it is a procedure to retry or a check to add, and the log should say which.
